I feel completely forced to spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting lighting, redoing my makeup, zooming in on photos, and constantly asking my friends for reassurance just to try to ease the overwhelming anxiety that everyone is judging how bloated and exhausted I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your primary issue is the distressing preoccupation with your appearance, or is it more about the compulsive behaviors you feel forced to perform to try to cope with these concerns?\n\nPatient: Honestly, they are deeply interconnected and both are completely taking over my life. The constant, obsessive fixation on my dark circles and bloated face is what starts the anxiety, which then drives me to do those exhausting things like spending 40 minutes on lighting and makeup or zooming in on photos. It feels like an endless cycle where the preoccupation triggers the behaviors, and I can't escape either one.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel and what you would do if you were in a situation where you couldn't perform your usual rituals, like adjusting the lighting or checking your appearance, before being seen or photographed?\n\nPatient: I would feel an intense wave of panic and would probably try to avoid the situation entirely, like turning off my camera or making an excuse to leave. If I was forced to be seen without preparing, I would be so incredibly self-conscious about my puffy face and dark circles that I wouldn't be able to focus on anything else, constantly worrying that everyone was judging me.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance concerns or engaging in these compulsive behaviors, and how does this impact your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: I easily spend several hours a day on this, between the 30 to 40 minutes I spend adjusting lighting and makeup before calls and then replaying the images in my head for hours afterward. This has completely stalled my career since I passed on a promotion and turned down leading webinars to avoid being on camera. It's also ruined my social life because I'm skipping parties and soccer games just to avoid having my photo taken.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your life would significantly improve and your anxiety would decrease if you could somehow magically resolve your appearance concerns, or do you feel like the compulsive behaviors themselves, such as the excessive preparation and reassurance seeking, are a major source of distress regardless of your appearance?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, but I feel like if I could just look \"normal\" and not have these flaws, I wouldn't have to do all this exhausting preparation and checking in the first place. If my face didn't look so bloated and uneven, I think the urge to do all those things would just go away. Right now, the urge to check my camera, adjust my makeup, and ask my friends for reassurance is so overwhelming that I can't imagine stopping. Even if I did manage to stop those things, I suspect the deep worry about my face looking bloated and uneven would still persist.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely stop worrying about what others think of your appearance, do you think you would still feel compelled to engage in your daily rituals of adjusting lighting, checking your appearance, and seeking reassurance?\n\nPatient: That is a really tough thing to separate, because while I am personally obsessed and distressed by seeing my puffy face and dark circles, a huge part of those rituals is driven by the intense fear of others judging me as looking exhausted and sloppy. I even turned down a big promotion and stopped leading webinars at work just to avoid having to be on video.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any intrusive, repetitive thoughts or urges to perform specific rituals or behaviors related to your appearance concerns, such as excessive mirror checking, excessive grooming, or mental acts to neutralize your perceived flaws?\n\nPatient: Yes, before any video call or event, I spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting the lighting, trying different angles, and redoing my makeup to cover up my puffy face and dark circles. During and after calls, I constantly check my camera box or zoom in on tagged photos, ask my friends for reassurance, and replay those images in my head for hours.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these repetitive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking or seeking reassurance, are something you feel driven to do to try to reduce your anxiety about your appearance, or are they more of a voluntary attempt to improve how you look?\n\nPatient: They definitely feel driven and compulsive rather than voluntary. I feel completely forced to spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting lighting, redoing my makeup, zooming in on photos, and constantly asking my friends for reassurance just to try to ease the overwhelming anxiety that everyone is judging how bloated and exhausted I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your primary issue is the distressing preoccupation with your appearance, or is it more about the compulsive behaviors you feel forced to perform to try to cope with these concerns?\n\nPatient: Honestly, they are deeply interconnected and both are completely taking over my life. The constant, obsessive fixation on my dark circles and bloated face is what starts the anxiety, which then drives me to do those exhausting things like spending 40 minutes on lighting and makeup or zooming in on photos. It feels like an endless cycle where the preoccupation triggers the behaviors, and I can't escape either one.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel and what you would do if you were in a situation where you couldn't perform your usual rituals, like adjusting the lighting or checking your appearance, before being seen or photographed?\n\nPatient: I would feel an intense wave of panic and would probably try to avoid the situation entirely, like turning off my camera or making an excuse to leave. If I was forced to be seen without preparing, I would be so incredibly self-conscious about my puffy face and dark circles that I wouldn't be able to focus on anything else, constantly worrying that everyone was judging me.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance concerns or engaging in these compulsive behaviors, and how does this impact your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: I easily spend several hours a day on this, between the 30 to 40 minutes I spend adjusting lighting and makeup before calls and then replaying the images in my head for hours afterward. This has completely stalled my career since I passed on a promotion and turned down leading webinars to avoid being on camera. It's also ruined my social life because I'm skipping parties and soccer games just to avoid having my photo taken.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your life would significantly improve and your anxiety would decrease if you could somehow magically resolve your appearance concerns, or do you feel like the compulsive behaviors themselves, such as the excessive preparation and reassurance seeking, are a major source of distress regardless of your appearance?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, but I feel like if I could just look \"normal\" and not have these flaws, I wouldn't have to do all this exhausting preparation and checking in the first place. If my face didn't look so bloated and uneven, I think the urge to do all those things would just go away. It really feels like the flaws themselves are the root of everything.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were able to stop performing these compulsive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking and reassurance seeking, your preoccupation with your appearance would significantly decrease, or would your concerns about your appearance persist regardless?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before. Right now, the urge to check my camera, adjust my makeup, and ask my friends for reassurance is so overwhelming that I can't imagine stopping. Even if I did manage to stop those things, I suspect the deep worry about my face looking bloated and uneven would still persist.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely stop worrying about what others think of your appearance, do you think you would still feel compelled to engage in your daily rituals of adjusting lighting, checking your appearance, and seeking reassurance?\n\nPatient: That is a really tough thing to separate, because while I am personally obsessed and distressed by seeing my puffy face and dark circles, a huge part of those rituals is driven by the intense fear of others judging me as looking exhausted and sloppy. If I truly didn't care about their reactions, I might still hate seeing the flaws myself, but the desperate need to constantly adjust the lighting, check the camera, and ask my friends for reassurance would probably lessen significantly.\n\nDoctor: If you were to experience a situation where your appearance concerns were completely validated, such as someone directly criticizing your looks, would your urge to perform these compulsive behaviors increase, decrease, or remain the same?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how my urges would change in that scenario, to be honest. I haven't really thought about how I would react if someone directly criticized me like that.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely eliminate your appearance concerns, do you think you would still feel the need to perform your daily rituals of checking and preparing, or would those behaviors stop as well?\n\nPatient: Oh, those rituals would definitely stop. All the time I spend adjusting the lighting, redoing my makeup, and zooming in on photos is entirely driven by my intense anxiety over my dark circles and bloated face. Without those worries, I wouldn't feel any need to do any of that.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to stop worrying about your appearance altogether, but still had the urge to perform your daily rituals, would you continue to do them, or are the rituals inextricably linked to your appearance concerns?\n\nPatient: They are absolutely linked; I would have no reason or urge to do them otherwise. All of those rituals—like spending 40 minutes on my makeup, adjusting the lighting, and zooming in on photos—are entirely about trying to hide or check my dark circles and bloated face. If I didn't have those worries about my appearance, the urge to do any of those things would completely disappear.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to stop performing your daily rituals without any negative consequences, do you think your preoccupation with your appearance would significantly decrease, or would you still find yourself obsessing over your perceived flaws?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, as I haven't thought about it that way before. It's so hard to even imagine not doing those rituals because the urge is so strong. I suspect I would still find myself obsessing over my face regardless, but it's difficult to say.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your obsessive focus on your appearance and the compulsive behaviors to cope with it are primarily aimed at preventing a specific, catastrophic outcome, such as being socially ostracized or professionally ruined, or are they more about alleviating a general sense of anxiety and discomfort related to your self-image?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. It feels like a mix of both, because I constantly worry about looking sloppy and unprofessional to others, but I also just have this deep, constant anxiety about my appearance whenever I see myself.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely accept your appearance as it is, without any attempts to change or hide it, would you still feel the need to perform your daily rituals of checking and preparing, or would those behaviors cease to be a problem for you?\n\nPatient: If I could truly accept my appearance, those exhausting rituals—like spending 40 minutes on my makeup, adjusting the lighting, and obsessively checking photos—would definitely stop, because I only do them to hide and check the flaws I'm fixated on. While it feels incredibly difficult to imagine actually accepting my face as it is right now, those behaviors are entirely driven by my obsession with my perceived flaws.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your obsessive focus on your appearance is more distressing to you, or is it the compulsive behaviors you feel forced to perform to cope with your appearance concerns that are more disturbing and disruptive to your life?\n\nPatient: Both are incredibly distressing and so closely linked. The obsessive thoughts, where I constantly replay images of my bloated face and dark circles, cause me absolute mental torment. But the compulsive behaviors—like spending 40 minutes on lighting and makeup, checking the camera, and zooming in on photos—are what physically consume my time and drive me to avoid my job and friends.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a situation where your obsessive thoughts about your appearance and the compulsive behaviors to cope with them are triggered by something other than being seen or photographed, such as a specific emotion, memory, or physical sensation?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed any other triggers besides those. Seeing myself on camera, preparing for video calls, or the fear of being photographed are the main things that seem to set off these thoughts and behaviors.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely eliminate your compulsive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking and reassurance seeking, do you think your preoccupation with your appearance would still be as distressing and time-consuming?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before. I suspect the distressing thoughts would still be there, but it's difficult to separate them.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any other obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors in your life that are unrelated to your appearance concerns?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think I've ever had other obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors unrelated to my appearance. My focus has really just been entirely on how I look on camera and in photos. I've started skipping parties, festivals, and even my soccer games because I dread the thought of people taking photos of me and tagging me on social media. I even turned down a big promotion and stopped leading webinars at work just to avoid having to be on video.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any intrusive, repetitive thoughts or urges to perform specific rituals or behaviors related to your appearance concerns, such as excessive mirror checking, excessive grooming, or mental acts to neutralize your perceived flaws?\n\nPatient: Yes, before any video call or event, I spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting the lighting, trying different angles, and redoing my makeup to cover up my puffy face and dark circles. During and after calls, I constantly check my camera box or zoom in on tagged photos, ask my friends for reassurance, and replay those images in my head for hours.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these repetitive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking or seeking reassurance, are something you feel driven to do to try to reduce your anxiety about your appearance, or are they more of a voluntary attempt to improve how you look?\n\nPatient: They definitely feel driven and compulsive rather than voluntary. I feel completely forced to spend 30 to 40 minutes adjusting lighting, redoing my makeup, zooming in on photos, and constantly asking my friends for reassurance just to try to ease the overwhelming anxiety that everyone is judging how bloated and exhausted I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your primary issue is the distressing preoccupation with your appearance, or is it more about the compulsive behaviors you feel forced to perform to try to cope with these concerns?\n\nPatient: Honestly, they are deeply interconnected and both are completely taking over my life. The constant, obsessive fixation on my dark circles and bloated face is what starts the anxiety, which then drives me to do those exhausting things like spending 40 minutes on lighting and makeup or zooming in on photos. It feels like an endless cycle where the preoccupation triggers the behaviors, and I can't escape either one.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you would feel and what you would do if you were in a situation where you couldn't perform your usual rituals, like adjusting the lighting or checking your appearance, before being seen or photographed?\n\nPatient: I would feel an intense wave of panic and would probably try to avoid the situation entirely, like turning off my camera or making an excuse to leave. If I was forced to be seen without preparing, I would be so incredibly self-conscious about my puffy face and dark circles that I wouldn't be able to focus on anything else, constantly worrying that everyone was judging me.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about your appearance concerns or engaging in these compulsive behaviors, and how does this impact your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: I easily spend several hours a day on this, between the 30 to 40 minutes I spend adjusting lighting and makeup before calls and then replaying the images in my head for hours afterward. This has completely stalled my career since I passed on a promotion and turned down leading webinars to avoid being on camera. It's also ruined my social life because I'm skipping parties and soccer games just to avoid having my photo taken.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your life would significantly improve and your anxiety would decrease if you could somehow magically resolve your appearance concerns, or do you feel like the compulsive behaviors themselves, such as the excessive preparation and reassurance seeking, are a major source of distress regardless of your appearance?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, but I feel like if I could just look \"normal\" and not have these flaws, I wouldn't have to do all this exhausting preparation and checking in the first place. If my face didn't look so bloated and uneven, I think the urge to do all those things would just go away. It really feels like the flaws themselves are the root of everything.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe that if you were able to stop performing these compulsive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking and reassurance seeking, your preoccupation with your appearance would significantly decrease, or would your concerns about your appearance persist regardless?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before. Right now, the urge to check my camera, adjust my makeup, and ask my friends for reassurance is so overwhelming that I can't imagine stopping. Even if I did manage to stop those things, I suspect the deep worry about my face looking bloated and uneven would still persist.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely stop worrying about what others think of your appearance, do you think you would still feel compelled to engage in your daily rituals of adjusting lighting, checking your appearance, and seeking reassurance?\n\nPatient: That is a really tough thing to separate, because while I am personally obsessed and distressed by seeing my puffy face and dark circles, a huge part of those rituals is driven by the intense fear of others judging me as looking exhausted and sloppy. If I truly didn't care about their reactions, I might still hate seeing the flaws myself, but the desperate need to constantly adjust the lighting, check the camera, and ask my friends for reassurance would probably lessen significantly.\n\nDoctor: If you were to experience a situation where your appearance concerns were completely validated, such as someone directly criticizing your looks, would your urge to perform these compulsive behaviors increase, decrease, or remain the same?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how my urges would change in that scenario, to be honest. I haven't really thought about how I would react if someone directly criticized me like that.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely eliminate your appearance concerns, do you think you would still feel the need to perform your daily rituals of checking and preparing, or would those behaviors stop as well?\n\nPatient: Oh, those rituals would definitely stop. If I didn't have those worries about my appearance, the urge to do any of those things would completely disappear.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to stop performing your daily rituals without any negative consequences, do you think your preoccupation with your appearance would significantly decrease, or would you still find yourself obsessing over your perceived flaws?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest, as I haven't thought about it that way before. It's so hard to even imagine not doing those rituals because the urge is so strong. I suspect I would still find myself obsessing over my face regardless, but it's difficult to say.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your obsessive focus on your appearance and the compulsive behaviors to cope with it are primarily aimed at preventing a specific, catastrophic outcome, such as being socially ostracized or professionally ruined, or are they more about alleviating a general sense of anxiety and discomfort related to your self-image?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. While it feels incredibly difficult to imagine actually accepting my face as it is right now, those behaviors are entirely driven by my obsession with my perceived flaws.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your obsessive focus on your appearance is more distressing to you, or is it the compulsive behaviors you feel forced to perform to cope with your appearance concerns that are more disturbing and disruptive to your life?\n\nPatient: Both are incredibly distressing and so closely linked. Seeing myself on camera, preparing for video calls, or the fear of being photographed are the main things that seem to set off these thoughts and behaviors.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely eliminate your compulsive behaviors, such as excessive mirror checking and reassurance seeking, do you think your preoccupation with your appearance would still be as distressing and time-consuming?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before.
